report:
Based on this research, the evidence actually supports the claim rather than contradicts it.

**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by evidence, not false.**

**Key evidence:**

1. **Tuuli et al., NEJM (2016)** — a large, well-conducted RCT (N=1,147) directly comparing chlorhexidine-alcohol vs. iodine-alcohol skin prep before cesarean delivery found a significantly lower surgical-site infection rate with chlorhexidine-alcohol (4.0% vs. 7.7%; RR ~0.52). This is the pivotal trial underlying the claim (https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

2. Additional RCTs have generally corroborated this direction, though with varying magnitude and some non-significant results (e.g., https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(17)30723-8/fulltext; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1198743X19303416).

3. **Cochrane systematic review (2020, updated pooling multiple RCTs)** concluded: "Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that preparing the skin with chlorhexidine gluconate before caesarean section is probably slightly more effective at reducing the incidence of surgical site infection in comparison to povidone iodine" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/; https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007462.pub5/abstract).

4. A more recent network meta-analysis of RCTs in cesarean sections likewise supports chlorhexidine's superiority, though acknowledging some fragility in the statistical results across concentrations and formulations (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195670124001282).

**Caveats:** The effect size is modest ("slightly more effective," per Cochrane), evidence certainty is "moderate" rather than high, not every individual trial reached statistical significance, and this is distinct from vaginal antisepsis research (a related but separate body of evidence).

**Bottom line:** The largest RCT and a Cochrane meta-analysis of multiple trials both support—not refute—the claim that chlorhexidine-alcohol modestly reduces surgical-site infection versus iodine-based preparations before cesarean delivery.
